- **A's total budget: 2000ms** (its SLA).
- Reserve, say, **~300ms** for A's own processing + serialization + a fallback path. That leaves ~1700ms for the call to B.
- **A→B timeout: ~1500ms** (inside the ~1700ms, with margin).
- B must reserve time for *its* own work; give B **~200ms**, leaving ~1300ms for its call to C.
- **B→C timeout: ~1000–1200ms**, strictly shorter than B's remaining budget.

So when C hangs, B's call to C times out (~1s), B returns/handles the error, and A still has headroom to run a fallback and answer within its 2s SLA — instead of blocking the full 2s and blowing it.

**The judgment:** the exact numbers matter less than the *nesting discipline* — each downstream timeout strictly smaller than the caller's remaining budget, with margin reserved at every hop. Pair timeouts with bounded retries (retries consume budget too) so a retry doesn't secretly blow the SLA.

**Common wrong answers:**
- "Shorter timeouts downstream" with no arithmetic showing they fit the budget.
- No timeout on A→B (the pile-up case).
- Ignoring that retries at any hop eat into the same budget.

**Taught in:** Timeout budgets; Retry with backoff and jitter.

drills.title: Choose your observability signal
drills.prompt: For each scenario, say whether logs, metrics, or traces are the right primary tool: (a) is the system healthy right now, (b) why was this one specific request slow across 4 services, (c) what exactly happened at 14:32:07 on host X.
drills.notes: (a) metrics, (b) traces, (c) logs. Bonus: note they're complementary, not substitutes -- a trace tells you which hop was slow, logs tell you why at that hop.
drills.solution:
**Crux:** For each scenario, name the right primary observability signal — logs, metrics, or traces — and note they're complementary.

**Position:** Map each scenario to the signal it's *for*:
- **(a) "Is the system healthy right now?"** → **Metrics.** Metrics are aggregated numeric time series (request rate, error rate, latency percentiles) — exactly what tells you overall health *now* and what you alert on.
- **(b) "Why was this one specific request slow across 4 services?"** → **Traces.** A trace follows the path of a *single* request across services, showing where time went at each hop — the right tool for "why was *this* request slow" in a distributed system.
- **(c) "What exactly happened at 14:32:07 on host X?"** → **Logs.** Logs are discrete, timestamped event records — best for "what exactly happened at this point."

**The bonus judgment the drill wants:** they're **complementary, not substitutes.** In practice you chain them: a metric alerts you that error rate spiked (health), a **trace** shows you *which hop* in the request was slow or failing, and **logs** at that hop tell you *why* it failed. Using only one leaves a gap — metrics can't tell you which request, traces can't tell you the low-level error detail, logs alone can't show the cross-service path.

**Common wrong answers:**
- Swapping traces and logs for (b)/(c) — logs don't reconstruct a cross-service path; traces don't carry every low-level detail.
- Treating them as interchangeable.
- Reaching for metrics to debug a single request (metrics are aggregates, not per-request).

**Taught in:** Observability and OpenTelemetry.

drills.title: Why OpenTelemetry over a vendor SDK
drills.prompt: Your team is choosing between instrumenting with a specific observability vendor's proprietary SDK vs. OpenTelemetry. Make the case for OTel, and name the actual switching-cost risk it avoids.
drills.notes: Vendor-neutral instrumentation avoids a re-instrumentation project if you switch backends later. Note OTel's 2025-2026 currency (all-signal GA in 2025, CNCF graduation in 2026) as a reason it's now the safe default, where a few years ago it might not have been mature enough.
drills.solution:
**Crux:** Make the case for instrumenting with **OpenTelemetry (OTel)** over a specific vendor's proprietary SDK, and name the switching-cost risk it avoids.

**Position:** Choose **OTel**. It gives you **one vendor-neutral instrumentation API across all three signals** — traces, metrics, and logs — plus a **Collector** that fans your data out to whatever backend you use (Datadog, Grafana, Honeycomb, CloudWatch). You instrument once, against open semantic conventions, and stay free to change *where* the data goes.

**The switching-cost risk it avoids (the specific answer):** if you instrument with a vendor's proprietary agent/SDK, your instrumentation is coupled to that vendor. **Switching observability vendors later becomes a full re-instrumentation project** — ripping out and rewriting instrumentation across every service. OTel decouples *how you instrument* from *which backend you pay*, so a vendor change becomes a Collector-config change, not a code rewrite.

**The currency/recency point that makes it the safe default *now*:** this is a datable shift. All three OTel signals reached **GA in 2025** (logs long lagged traces and metrics), and OTel **graduated as a CNCF project in 2026**, described as "the de facto standard for open source observability" with the second-highest project velocity after Kubernetes. So a few years ago the maturity caveat was real; in 2026 it's the safe default rather than a bet.

**Common wrong answers:**
- Picking the vendor SDK "for tighter integration/less setup" while ignoring lock-in.
- Claiming OTel is too immature — true years ago, not after 2025 all-signal GA / 2026 graduation.
- Missing the concrete risk (re-instrumentation cost) and arguing only "open is nicer."

**Taught in:** Observability and OpenTelemetry.

drills.title: Design an API versioning strategy for a public API
drills.prompt: You're launching a public API used by external third parties you don't control. Choose a versioning strategy (URI, header, date-based) and design a deprecation policy for when v1 needs to go away.
drills.notes: For public/external clients, URI versioning is the pragmatic default (visible, cache-friendly). Deprecation policy should include real dates and a Sunset header, not a silent cutover.
drills.solution:
**Crux:** Choose an API versioning strategy for a *public* API used by external third parties you don't control, and design a deprecation policy for retiring v1.

**Position:** For public/external clients, use **URI versioning** (`/v1/orders`) as the pragmatic default. The reasons matter: it's **visible**, **cache-friendly**, and **trivially routable at a gateway** — all of which help when you don't control the clients. Header-based versioning is better for *internal* services where you own every client (URIs stay stable), but its classic failure — clients forgetting to send the header and silently defaulting to "latest," quietly breaking — is exactly the risk you can't afford with third parties you can't coordinate with. Date-based versioning is a reasonable alternative for APIs shipping frequent additive changes, but URI is the safe public default.

**Deprecation policy (the design the drill wants):**
- **Version only for genuinely breaking changes** — prefer backward-compatible, additive evolution, since every version is a maintenance cost you carry.
- **Announce with real dates**, not a vague "soon."
- **Use the `Sunset` HTTP header** where applicable to signal the retirement date programmatically.
- **Give a genuine migration window** — a real overlap where v1 and v2 both work — rather than a silent cutover. External clients need time to migrate on their own schedules.

**Common wrong answers:**
- Header-based versioning for uncontrolled external clients — the "forgot the header, silently got latest" trap.
- A silent/immediate v1 cutover with no window or `Sunset` header.
- Versioning on every change (including additive) — needless maintenance burden.

**Taught in:** API versioning and evolution.

drills.title: The 'additive change' trap
drills.prompt: A teammate says 'we're just adding a new required field to the response, that's backward compatible, no version bump needed.' Are they right? What about adding a new enum value to an existing field?
drills.notes: Both are traps: a new REQUIRED field can break strict client-side schema validation; a new enum value can break a client's switch/case that doesn't have a default branch. 'Additive' isn't automatically 'safe.'
drills.solution:
**Crux:** Is "we're just adding a new *required* field to the response, so it's backward compatible, no version bump" correct? And what about adding a new enum value to an existing field?

**Position:** **Both are traps** — the teammate is wrong. "Additive" is *not* the same as "safe." The rule: adding a new *optional* field or a new endpoint is generally safe; but changing existing behaviour in a way old clients don't expect is breaking, **even if the JSON shape looks unchanged.**

- **New *required* field in the response:** a client doing **strict schema validation** may reject a response that contains a field its schema doesn't know about, or (if "required" is enforced on requests too) start failing when the field it must now send is absent. Either way it can break existing clients despite "just adding." A *required* field is precisely the case the lesson calls out as breaking-despite-additive.
- **New enum value on an existing field:** breaks a client whose **switch/case (or exhaustive match) has no default branch** — it encounters a value it was never coded to handle and errors or misbehaves. The shape didn't change, but the *domain of values* did.

**The judgment the drill wants:** distinguish "the JSON structure is unchanged" from "old clients can still correctly process it." Safety is about what clients *do* with the data, not just the field list. When in doubt about strict validators or non-defaulting switches, treat it as breaking and version it.

**Common wrong answers:**
- Agreeing that any additive change is automatically safe.
- Thinking only structural changes (rename/remove/type change) are breaking, missing required-field and new-enum-value cases.
- "Clients should just handle unknown values" — true in principle, but you don't control external clients, so you can't assume it.

**Taught in:** API versioning and evolution.

drills.title: Feature flag vs. rollback plan
drills.prompt: You're about to ship a risky change. Compare shipping it behind a feature flag vs. relying on your deploy pipeline's rollback. Why might you want both?
drills.notes: Flag gives instant kill-switch without a redeploy; rollback is the fallback if the flag itself doesn't fully contain the blast radius (e.g. a schema migration that shipped alongside it). Watch for over-reliance on flags as a permanent substitute for real rollback.
drills.solution:
**Crux:** Shipping a risky change behind a **feature flag** vs relying on the deploy pipeline's **rollback** — and why you might want both.

**Position:** They solve *different* problems, so use both.
- A **feature flag decouples deploy from release.** You ship the code to production **dark**, then turn it on for a subset of traffic (internal users, a percentage rollout, a specific tenant) independent of the deploy pipeline. Its key power here is the **boolean kill-switch**: if the feature misbehaves, flip it off **without a redeploy** — the fastest possible rollback path for the *feature*.
- A **deploy rollback** reverts the *deployed artifact* — it's your fallback when the problem isn't cleanly contained by a flag.

**Why you want both (the judgment):** a flag only contains what the flag actually gates. If the risky change shipped **alongside something a flag can't toggle back** — e.g. a **schema migration** that went out with the deploy — flipping the flag off doesn't undo the migration, and you need the deploy rollback (or a forward fix) for that. So the flag handles fast, redeploy-free containment of the feature *logic*, and the rollback covers the blast radius the flag can't reach.

**The trap to name:** don't treat a flag as a *permanent* substitute for a real rollback path or deploy hygiene — a flag is a *temporary* decoupling mechanism. Over-reliance leads to **flag debt** (flags that outlive their purpose, leaving dead branches and a combinatorial test surface). Give every flag an owner and an expiry.

**Common wrong answers:**
- "Flags replace rollbacks" — they don't cover un-gated changes like migrations.
- "Rollback is enough, skip the flag" — loses the instant, redeploy-free kill-switch and gradual rollout.
- Ignoring flag debt / no expiry.

**Taught in:** Feature flags; Blue-green, canary, and rolling (rollback context).

drills.title: Canary vs blue-green for a stateful service
drills.prompt: You're deploying a new version of a service that owns a shared database with a schema change. Would you use canary or blue-green, and what does the schema change force you to do regardless of which you pick?
drills.notes: Either way, the schema must support BOTH old and new code running simultaneously during the rollout (expand/contract migration pattern) -- the deployment pattern choice doesn't remove the backward-compatibility requirement.
drills.solution:
**Crux:** Deploying a new version of a service that owns a shared database *with a schema change* — canary or blue-green? And what does the schema change force regardless of which you pick?

**Position:** The **key insight the drill wants** is that the deployment pattern choice doesn't remove the hard constraint: **during any rollout, both old and new code run at once** against the *same* database, so the schema must be compatible with **both versions simultaneously.** That forces the **expand/contract (parallel-change) migration pattern** no matter what:
1. **Expand** — add the new schema elements in a backward-compatible way (new nullable column/table), deploy code that writes both old and new;
2. roll out the new version;
3. **Contract** — only after the old version is fully gone, remove the old schema elements.

**Pattern choice:**
- **Canary** — release to a small slice of real traffic first, watch error rate/latency, widen if healthy or roll back fast. Lowest blast radius, but needs good real-time observability. With a shared DB, both versions are *definitely* live during the canary, so expand/contract is mandatory.
- **Blue-green** — two full environments, switch traffic at the router at once; instant rollback by flipping back. But the **shared stateful database still needs its own compatibility story** — the "instant flip" doesn't apply to the data, and if green's code assumed a contracted schema you can't safely flip back to blue.

**The judgment:** for a schema-changing stateful service, either pattern works *only* on top of expand/contract; the choice is about traffic blast-radius and rollback speed, not about escaping the backward-compatibility requirement. Canary suits gradual validation with strong observability; blue-green suits fast full-cutover with instant traffic rollback — but neither makes the DB migration safe by itself.

**Common wrong answers:**
- Assuming blue-green's instant flip covers the database too — it doesn't; state is shared.
- Doing a single destructive migration (drop/rename) during rollout — breaks the version still running.
- Picking a pattern without mentioning expand/contract at all.

**Taught in:** Blue-green, canary, and rolling; API versioning and evolution (backward-compatible evolution / expand-contract thinking).

drills.title: SDE2 framing: 'design a rate limiter' -- name the cross-cutting concerns
drills.prompt: Design a rate limiter service. Beyond the core algorithm (token bucket, sliding window), what resilience and observability concerns would you raise unprompted to signal SDE2-level depth?
drills.notes: Look for unprompted mentions of: what happens when the rate limiter's own backing store (Redis) is slow/down (fail open vs fail closed -- a resilience trade-off), metrics on throttling rate, and a timeout budget for the limiter check itself so it doesn't become the slowest hop in the request path.
drills.solution:
**Crux:** Beyond the core algorithm (token bucket, sliding window), what **resilience and observability** concerns would you raise *unprompted* when designing a rate limiter, to signal SDE2 depth?

**Position:** The algorithm is table stakes; SDE2 signal comes from the cross-cutting concerns you raise without being asked:

- **What happens when the rate limiter's own backing store is slow or down?** A distributed limiter usually keeps counters in a shared store (e.g. Redis). If that store degrades, the limiter itself becomes a failure point. You must make an explicit **fail-open vs fail-closed** decision: **fail open** (allow traffic when the limiter can't check) protects availability but drops the protection; **fail closed** (reject when you can't check) preserves protection but can cause an outage of its own. This is a resilience tradeoff, and *naming it unprompted* is the tell.
- **A timeout budget for the limiter check itself.** The limiter sits in the request hot path, so its check needs an explicit, tight **timeout** — otherwise a slow store makes the limiter the *slowest hop* in every request, i.e. the limiter becomes the latency problem it was meant to prevent. Reserve only a small slice of the caller's budget for the check.
- **Observability:** emit **metrics on throttling rate** (how many requests are being rejected, per client/tenant) so you can tell "working as intended" from "misconfigured and rejecting good traffic," and alert on it. Traces help confirm the limiter check isn't dominating request latency.

**The judgment:** a rate limiter is a small system that touches *every* request, so its own resilience (store failure mode, timeout) and observability matter as much as the algorithm. Consider a **bulkhead / per-tenant** limit so one abusive tenant can't consume shared capacity.

**Common wrong answers:**
- Only discussing token bucket vs sliding window and stopping.
- Ignoring the limiter's own failure mode (no fail-open/closed decision).
- No timeout on the limiter check — it silently becomes the slowest hop.

**Taught in:** Retry with backoff and jitter / Timeout budgets; Circuit breaker (fail-fast/fallback thinking); Bulkhead and cell-based isolation; Observability and OpenTelemetry.

drills.title: Synthesis: pick the architecture for a new greenfield product
drills.prompt: You're the most senior engineer on a 6-person team building a new B2B SaaS product from scratch, expecting moderate but uncertain growth. Walk through your architecture choice (monolith vs modular monolith vs microservices), your service/module boundaries, and the first two cross-cutting concerns (from resilience/observability) you'd invest in on day one.
drills.notes: Expected default: modular monolith, boundaries drawn from anticipated bounded contexts (not yet real team splits), and day-one investment in basic observability (structured logging + OTel from the start) over premature resilience machinery (circuit breakers) the team doesn't need yet at this scale.
drills.solution:
**Crux:** Senior engineer on a 6-person team, greenfield B2B SaaS, moderate-but-uncertain growth. Choose the architecture, draw the boundaries, and name the first two cross-cutting concerns to invest in on day one.

**Position (architecture):** Default to a **modular monolith** — a single deployable unit internally partitioned into modules with **enforced boundaries**. It gives you the boundary discipline of microservices without the distributed-systems tax, which is exactly right for a 6-person team with *uncertain* growth: you can't yet name a forcing function (independent team scaling, independent deploy cadence, a real per-service scaling bottleneck) that would justify microservices. Splitting into network-connected services now would just be "a monolith with extra HTTP calls," strictly worse. If real pain appears later, well-drawn modules are cheap to extract into services.

**Boundaries:** draw modules around **anticipated bounded contexts / business capabilities** (e.g. identity, billing, the core product domain), *not* around premature team splits — with 6 engineers you don't yet have distinct teams, and Conway's Law warns against freezing in the wrong org-shaped boundaries early. Keep aggregates small and reference across modules by ID.

**First two cross-cutting concerns on day one:** invest in **basic observability first** — **structured logging plus OpenTelemetry instrumentation from the start** (traces/metrics/logs), because retrofitting instrumentation later is a re-instrumentation project, and OTel is now the vendor-neutral safe default. Second, lightweight **API/contract hygiene and expand/contract-friendly evolution** between modules so boundaries stay clean.

**The judgment the drill wants:** *don't* prematurely build resilience machinery (circuit breakers, bulkheads, sagas) — at this scale, in-process calls in a monolith don't need them yet, and adding them is ceremony for problems you don't have. Observability pays off immediately; heavy resilience patterns are earned by distributed pain you haven't felt.

**Common wrong answers:**
- Microservices "to be ready for scale" — no forcing function; premature distributed tax.
- Day-one circuit breakers/sagas in a monolith that makes in-process calls.
- Drawing module boundaries around imagined team splits rather than bounded contexts.

**Taught in:** Microservices vs modular monolith (2025-26); Bounded contexts; Where to draw the boundary; Conway's Law; Observability and OpenTelemetry.

drills.title: Design a URL Shortener (Bitly)
drills.prompt: Design a service that shortens long URLs and redirects short codes to the original URL at scale. Cover ID/code generation, read-heavy caching, and redirect type (301 vs 302) tradeoffs.
drills.notes: Good warm-up problem. Focus on base62 encoding vs hashing for code generation, and cache-aside in front of the key-value store.
drills.solution:
**Requirements.** Functional: create a short code for a long URL; redirect a short code to its original URL. Non-functional: reads dominate writes ~1000:1, redirects under ~100ms, high availability (a stale/unavailable redirect is worse than a rejected create).

**Core entities + API.** Entity: `Url{ code, long_url, created_at }`.
```
POST /urls {long_url}  -> {short_url}
GET  /{code}           -> 302 redirect
```

**High-level design.** A stateless app tier behind a load balancer writes/reads a key-value store keyed by `code` (get-by-code is the only access pattern, so a KV store like DynamoDB is the honest SQL-vs-NoSQL choice). Code generation: take a **unique ID generator** (Snowflake-style, no coordination) and base62-encode it — this avoids the "two shards both emit code X" collision you'd get from per-shard auto-increment. Hashing the URL is the alternative but needs collision handling.

**Deep dive 1 — read path caching.** Redirects are extremely read-heavy, so put **cache-aside** (Redis) in front of the KV store: on a miss, load and populate with a TTL. Mappings are immutable, so invalidation is a non-problem — the hard part of caching disappears here. A CDN/edge cache can serve popular codes even closer to the user.

**Deep dive 2 — 301 vs 302 tradeoff.** A **301 (permanent)** lets the browser and intermediary caches remember the mapping, which offloads your service — but you then lose click analytics and can never repoint the code. A **302 (temporary)** forces every click through your service (analytics, ability to change the target) at the cost of more traffic. Most shorteners choose 302 for exactly the control it preserves.

Taught in: A framework that fits in 45 minutes; Unique ID generation; SQL vs NoSQL; Caching; CDNs, edge caching & DNS; Estimation, only when it changes the design.

drills.title: Design a Distributed Rate Limiter
drills.prompt: Design a rate limiter usable across many API server instances that limits requests per user/IP/API key. Justify your algorithm choice (token bucket vs sliding window vs leaky bucket) and how you enforce it atomically in a distributed setting.
drills.notes: Common SDE2 favorite because it's self-contained. Know why per-node counting alone breaks under multiple instances.
drills.solution:
**Requirements.** Functional: allow/deny a request based on a per-user/IP/API-key quota, enforced consistently across many app instances. Non-functional: sub-millisecond decision, correct under concurrency, fail-open vs fail-closed decided deliberately.

**Core entities + API.** The limiter is middleware, not a user-facing API. Conceptually: `allow(key) -> bool`, backed by counter/bucket state per `key`.

**High-level design.** Enforce at the **API gateway** (the taught single front door for cross-cutting concerns like rate limiting) so limits apply before requests fan out to services. The critical insight from the fundamentals: **a per-server counter is not a real limit behind a load balancer** — three instances each allowing N gives 3N. State must live in one shared store, so the buckets live in **Redis** where all app servers share one view.

**Deep dive 1 — algorithm choice.** The taught rate-limiting lesson gives three:
- **Fixed window** — simplest, but allows a 2x burst at the window boundary.
- **Sliding window** — smooths that boundary by weighting the previous window.
- **Token bucket** — refills at a steady rate up to a cap; cap = burst tolerance, refill rate = sustained limit. This is the usual answer because it permits short legitimate bursts while bounding sustained rate.
Pick token bucket for a public API (bursty but bounded); a sliding window when boundary bursts are unacceptable.

**Deep dive 2 — atomicity in a distributed setting.** Read-then-write on the counter is racy across instances. Make the check-and-decrement **atomic** in Redis (a single server-side script), so concurrent requests can't both consume the last token. This is the distributed-lock lesson's preferred escape hatch: rather than a distributed lock, give each key a single owner (the one Redis shard) and make the mutation atomic.

Taught in: Rate limiting; API gateways & service discovery; Load balancers & reverse proxies; Concurrency control (optimistic, pessimistic & distributed locks); Caching.

drills.title: Design a News Feed (Facebook/Twitter-style)
drills.prompt: Design a system where users follow other users and see a feed of posts from people they follow. Address the 'celebrity problem' where a small number of accounts have millions of followers.
drills.notes: The fan-out-on-write vs fan-out-on-read vs hybrid decision is the whole interview. Ranking is a secondary layer, don't over-invest there first.
drills.solution:
**Requirements.** Functional: users follow users; a user reads a feed of recent posts from those they follow; users create posts. Non-functional: feed reads are extremely read-heavy and must be fast; the system must survive a celebrity with tens of millions of followers.

**Core entities + API.** `User`, `Post{id, author, body, created_at}`, `Follow{follower, followee}`.
```
POST /posts {body}
GET  /feed?cursor=...  -> [post]
```
Derive the current user from the auth token, never the body.

**High-level design.** Post IDs come from a **Snowflake-style ID generator** — time-sortable, so a feed is a descending scan by id with no separate sort. Writes go to a primary; feed reads scale on **read replicas**.

**Deep dive 1 — fan-out (the whole interview).** The taught feed fan-out lesson frames it exactly:
- **Fan-out on write (push):** on post, insert the post id into every follower's precomputed feed. Reads become trivial. Breaks when a celebrity posts and one write becomes 50M writes — the fan-out storm / hot-key problem.
- **Fan-out on read (pull):** store the post once; gather-and-merge at read time. Cheap writes, expensive reads.
- **Hybrid (the strong answer):** push for normal users, pull for the handful of celebrities, merge at read time. Name it *and* why.

**Deep dive 2 — caching the feed.** Precomputed feeds live in a **cache** (Redis lists) with cache-aside repopulation; ranking is a thin layer applied at read time and is deliberately secondary — don't over-invest before the fan-out decision is made.

Taught in: Feed fan-out: push vs pull; Unique ID generation; Connection pooling & read replicas; Caching; A framework that fits in 45 minutes.

drills.title: Design a Chat System (WhatsApp/Discord-style)
drills.prompt: Design a messaging system supporting 1:1 and group chats with delivery receipts, presence, and effectively infinite message history. Explain your partition key choice and how you'd avoid hot partitions on popular channels.
drills.notes: Study the real Discord Cassandra->ScyllaDB migration in 03-case-studies.md before attempting -- request coalescing and consistent hashing are the senior-level deep dive here.
drills.solution:
**Requirements.** Functional: 1:1 and group messages, delivery receipts, presence, effectively infinite history. Non-functional: low-latency delivery, ordered per conversation, must not create hot partitions on popular channels.

**Core entities + API.** `Message{id, channel_id, sender, body, ts}`, `Channel`, `Membership`.
```
send(channel_id, body)
GET /channels/{id}/messages?before=cursor
```

**High-level design.** Real-time delivery uses **WebSockets** (the taught standard for chat) — a persistent bidirectional connection. Because a socket is **stateful and lives on one server**, you need a **connection registry** (which user is on which server, in Redis) plus a pub/sub layer so any server can publish to the server holding the target connection. Message IDs are **Snowflake-style**, giving per-channel time ordering for free.

**Deep dive 1 — storage & partition key.** History is write-heavy and append-only — a **wide-column** store (Cassandra/ScyllaDB) fits the query-first schema. The taught replication-and-partitioning lesson is the crux: partition by `channel_id` and a time **bucket**, e.g. `(channel_id, day)`, so writes distribute and a single channel's history doesn't grow one partition unbounded. A good *write*-distributing key can still be a bad *read* key — a huge popular channel concentrates reads on the current bucket (a **hot partition**), which is exactly why you bucket by time and can add read replicas.

**Deep dive 2 — delivery guarantees.** Delivery is **at-least-once**, so consumers/clients must be **idempotent** (dedupe by message id). Fan-out to group members reuses the push/pull tension from feeds: push into per-member inboxes for small groups, pull for very large channels.

Taught in: Real-time delivery; Replication and partitioning; Unique ID generation; SQL vs NoSQL; Message queues and streams; Feed fan-out: push vs pull; Connection pooling & read replicas.

drills.title: Design a Video Streaming Platform (YouTube-style)
drills.prompt: Design video upload, transcoding, and playback at scale. The core bottleneck is egress bandwidth to viewers, not storage -- design around that.
drills.notes: Don't skip the async transcoding pipeline. CDN placement in front of blob storage is the key deep dive.
drills.solution:
**Requirements.** Functional: upload a video, transcode to multiple renditions, play back smoothly worldwide. Non-functional: the core bottleneck is **egress bandwidth to viewers**, not storage; upload/transcode can be asynchronous; playback latency and buffering must be low.

**Core entities + API.** `Video{id, owner, status, renditions[]}`.
```
POST /videos (initiate upload) -> upload URL
GET  /videos/{id}/manifest     -> rendition list
```

**High-level design.** The upload returns fast, then heavy work happens off the request path. This is the taught **message-queue** pattern: the API enqueues a "transcode job" and returns 202 Accepted; **workers** dequeue and transcode into multiple bitrates asynchronously. Raw and transcoded files land in blob storage.

**Deep dive 1 — CDN in front of blob storage (the key deep dive).** Egress dominates, so you never stream from origin. Push renditions to a **CDN** so each viewer is served from a **point of presence** near them — this cuts latency (fewer/shorter hops) and offloads the enormous read traffic from your servers, which is the whole game for video. Content-hashed rendition URLs sidestep the CDN's invalidation problem.

**Deep dive 2 — async pipeline & idempotency.** Transcoding is slow and bursty; the queue provides **backpressure** so upload spikes don't overwhelm workers. Delivery is at-least-once, so a worker re-processing a job must be **idempotent** (keyed by video id + rendition) to avoid duplicate outputs. Playback itself is HTTP over a CDN, benefiting from **HTTP/2/3** multiplexing for the many small segment requests.

Taught in: Message queues and streams; CDNs, edge caching & DNS; TCP/UDP, HTTP/2 & 3, gRPC, webhooks; A framework that fits in 45 minutes.

drills.title: Design a Ride-Sharing Dispatch System (Uber-style)
drills.prompt: Design a system that ingests constant driver location updates and matches riders to nearby available drivers with low latency. Justify your geospatial indexing choice.
drills.notes: Read the actual Uber H3 blog post. Know why hexagons (uniform neighbor distance) beat geohash squares and quadtrees for this specific dispatch use case.
drills.solution:
**Requirements.** Functional: drivers continuously report location; match a rider to a nearby available driver with low latency. Non-functional: extremely write-heavy on location updates, low-latency proximity matching, geographically distributed.

**Core entities + API.** `Driver{id, location, available}`, `Ride{id, rider, driver, status}`.
```
POST /drivers/{id}/location {lat,lng}   (very high frequency)
POST /rides/request {rider_location}    -> matched driver
```

**High-level design.** Location updates are a firehose. Ingest them through a **stream (Kafka)** so the write burst is absorbed with **backpressure** and multiple consumers (matching, analytics, ETA) read independently at their own offsets. Current driver positions live in an in-memory store (Redis) keyed by a spatial cell for fast proximity lookup.

**Deep dive 1 — geospatial indexing (the justification the prompt wants).** You bucket the map into cells and index drivers by cell so "find nearby" reads only a handful of cells instead of scanning everyone. Uber's H3 hexagonal grid is the real-world choice because hexagons give **uniform neighbor distance**, which matters for a dispatch/expansion search (ring-by-ring outward) far more than for a one-shot lookup. (Grounded in the drill's own H3 source; the taught concept underneath is choosing a partition/index scheme by access pattern.)

**Deep dive 2 — write scale & hot cells.** Per the taught partitioning lesson, a dense downtown cell is a **hot partition** for both writes and reads. Mitigate by keeping only latest-position-per-driver (idempotent overwrite, not append) and by treating location state as **AP** (CAP): a driver dot that's a second stale is fine, so favour availability and low latency over strict consistency on positions.

Taught in: Message queues and streams; Replication and partitioning; CAP and PACELC; Caching; A framework that fits in 45 minutes.

drills.title: Design a Payment System
drills.prompt: Design a system that charges a payer and credits a payee via an external payment processor, guaranteeing money is never lost or duplicated despite retries and network failures.
drills.notes: Read Stripe's own idempotency blog post -- it's the single best primary source. Double-entry ledger + idempotency keys + integer cents are the three load-bearing decisions.
drills.solution:
**Requirements.** Functional: charge a payer, credit a payee via an external processor. Non-functional (the hard ones): money is never lost or double-charged despite client retries, timeouts, and processor failures; strong consistency on balances.

**Core entities + API.** `Payment{id, payer, payee, amount_cents, status}`, ledger entries.
```
POST /payments {payer, payee, amount, idempotency_key}
```
Store money as integer **cents**, never floats.

**High-level design.** Payments are the archetypal **CP** system from the CAP lesson: during a partition you must **refuse or block** rather than risk an inconsistent charge — a wrong answer is worse than no answer. Balances live in a relational DB with **ACID transactions** (SQL-vs-NoSQL: this is squarely the "relationships + transactions → relational" case).

**Deep dive 1 — idempotency (the load-bearing decision).** The client may retry after a timeout without knowing whether the first attempt succeeded. Require an **idempotency key** per payment: store `key -> result`; on a duplicate key, return the stored result instead of charging again. This is the same at-least-once discipline the queues and webhooks lessons demand — the processor's callbacks are at-least-once too, so your handler must dedupe.

**Deep dive 2 — concurrency on balances.** Two concurrent debits on one account race. Use **concurrency control** from the taught lesson: pessimistic `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` when contention is high (scarce balance), or optimistic version-check with retry when conflicts are rare. A double-entry ledger (every movement is two balanced rows) makes correctness auditable.

Taught in: CAP and PACELC; SQL vs NoSQL; Concurrency control (optimistic, pessimistic & distributed locks); Message queues and streams; TCP/UDP, HTTP/2 & 3, gRPC, webhooks.

drills.title: Design a Notification System
drills.prompt: Design a system that delivers notifications (push, email, SMS, in-app) triggered by product events to potentially millions of users, respecting per-user preferences and avoiding duplicate delivery.
drills.notes: Reuses the fan-out pattern from news feed. The interesting part is per-channel failure isolation and idempotent delivery workers.
drills.solution:
**Requirements.** Functional: deliver notifications across channels (push, email, SMS, in-app) triggered by product events, respecting per-user preferences, without duplicates. Non-functional: scale to millions of recipients, isolate per-channel failures, at-least-once delivery made safe.

**Core entities + API.** `Notification{id, user, channel, payload, status}`, `Preference{user, channel, enabled}`.
```
emit(event)  (internal) -> fan out to recipients' enabled channels
```

**High-level design.** A product event lands on a **stream (Kafka)**; a fan-out step expands it to recipients (reusing the **feed fan-out** pattern) and enqueues one job per (user, channel). Per-channel **worker** pools (SQS-style task queues) pull jobs and call the provider. The queue gives **backpressure** so an event spike doesn't overwhelm downstream providers.

**Deep dive 1 — per-channel failure isolation.** Separate queues per channel mean a flaky SMS provider can't back up email or push. A dead-letter queue captures repeated failures for retry/inspection. This is the queues lesson's decoupling applied so one slow consumer doesn't block the request path or the other channels.

**Deep dive 2 — idempotent, non-duplicate delivery.** Delivery is **at-least-once**, so a redelivered job must not send twice: workers dedupe on `notification_id` (idempotency), the same discipline taught for queues and webhooks. Preferences are a simple read that fits a **cache-aside** lookup since they change rarely.


**Extra tradeoff.** Batching vs latency: coalescing many events for one user into a single digest cuts provider calls but delays delivery, so let per-user preferences decide the batch window. Ordering across channels is not guaranteed and shouldn't be relied on.
Taught in: Message queues and streams; Feed fan-out: push vs pull; Caching; TCP/UDP, HTTP/2 & 3, gRPC, webhooks; A framework that fits in 45 minutes.

drills.title: Design a Web Crawler
drills.prompt: Design a crawler that discovers and downloads pages starting from seed URLs while respecting per-host politeness (robots.txt, crawl-delay) and avoiding re-crawling duplicates.
drills.notes: Politeness is fundamentally a per-host queueing/sharding problem, not a global rate limit. Bloom filters for URL dedup at scale.
drills.solution:
**Requirements.** Functional: from seed URLs, discover and download pages, follow links, avoid re-crawling duplicates, respect per-host politeness (robots.txt, crawl-delay). Non-functional: high throughput without hammering any single host; resumable; bounded dedup memory.

**Data flow (this is a pipeline system, so the optional data-flow step applies).** seed URLs → frontier queue → fetch → parse → extract links → enqueue new URLs → repeat.

**High-level design.** The frontier is a **message queue/stream**: fetchers are **workers** dequeuing URLs, and newly discovered links are enqueued back. The queue provides **backpressure** so parsing can't outrun fetching.

**Deep dive 1 — per-host politeness as partitioning.** Politeness is not a global rate limit; it's a **per-host** constraint. Partition the frontier **by host** (the taught partition-key idea) so each host maps to a single queue/worker that applies that host's crawl-delay — the same "give each key a single owner" move used to avoid distributed locks. This also prevents one giant site from becoming a **hot partition** that starves others.

**Deep dive 2 — dedup at scale.** You must not re-crawl a URL you've seen. Maintain a seen-set; at small scale a DB with an **index** on the normalized URL suffices, and query optimization matters (this is a `WHERE url = ?` lookup that must hit the index, not a scan). **Rate limiting** per host caps request rate politely. Content that changes over time gets a re-crawl TTL, echoing cache-invalidation reasoning.


**Extra tradeoff.** Freshness vs cost: a shorter re-crawl TTL keeps the index current but multiplies fetch load and pressures per-host politeness limits, so tune it per content type (news pages short, static docs long).
Taught in: Message queues and streams; Replication and partitioning; Rate limiting; Indexing, query optimization & N+1; Caching.

drills.title: Design Typeahead / Autocomplete
drills.prompt: Design a search-box autocomplete feature returning top-K ranked completions per keystroke in well under 100ms, backed by a constantly-changing corpus of search term popularity.
drills.notes: Trie with precomputed top-K per node is the standard answer. Explain the offline batch job that refreshes popularity counts.
drills.solution:
**Requirements.** Functional: return top-K ranked completions for a prefix on every keystroke, from a corpus of search-term popularity. Non-functional: p99 well under 100ms (the tail is what users feel while typing), read-heavy, corpus popularity changes constantly but not instantly.

**Core entities + API.** `Completion{prefix, suggestions[], score}`.
```
GET /autocomplete?prefix=...  -> top-K completions
```

**High-level design.** This is a pure read-latency problem, so precompute. An **offline batch job** (a stream/queue-fed pipeline) aggregates raw search logs into popularity counts and materializes **top-K completions per prefix**. The online path is then a single fast lookup by prefix.

**Deep dive 1 — serving latency (caching + read replicas).** Serve the precomputed top-K from a **cache** (Redis) with **cache-aside**; popular prefixes stay hot. Because it's read-heavy, back the cache with **read replicas** to scale reads horizontally. The taught **latency/tail-latency** lesson is the target: optimise p99, since one page fires a request per keystroke and the slowest dominates the felt experience.

**Deep dive 2 — freshness tradeoff (invalidation).** New/trending terms shouldn't require a full recompute per keystroke. Refresh the materialized completions on a schedule (offline job) and use a **TTL** on cached entries — the exact caching invalidation tradeoff: a short TTL means fresher suggestions but more recompute/load; a longer TTL serves slightly stale rankings cheaply. The lookup itself is a keyed read (KV-shaped), so SQL-vs-NoSQL favours a key-value store here.

Taught in: Caching; Connection pooling & read replicas; Latency, tail latency & multi-region; Message queues and streams; SQL vs NoSQL; Estimation, only when it changes the design.

drills.title: Design Ticketmaster (Event Ticketing)
drills.prompt: Design an event ticketing system that lets users browse events and book seats, guaranteeing no seat is ever double-sold even during a flash-sale traffic spike for a popular event.
drills.notes: Canonical CAP-theorem-by-feature example: strong consistency for booking, availability for browsing. Seat-hold TTL design is the key deep dive.
drills.solution:
**Requirements.** Functional: browse events, view seats, book a seat. Non-functional: **no seat is ever double-sold**, even under a flash-sale spike; browsing stays available and fast.

**Core entities + API.** `Event`, `Seat{id, event_id, status}`, `Booking{id, user, seats[]}`.
```
GET  /events/{id}/seats
POST /seats/{id}/hold   -> hold with TTL
POST /bookings          -> confirm held seats
```

**High-level design.** This is the taught **CAP-by-feature** split, textbook version:
- **Booking is CP** — a double-sold seat is catastrophic, so during a partition you refuse/block rather than risk it. Seats live in a relational DB with **ACID transactions** (SQL-vs-NoSQL: transactions + correctness → relational).
- **Browsing is AP** — showing a slightly stale "available" count is fine; serve it from **read replicas** and a **cache** (accept lag) so the browse path stays up and fast under load.

**Deep dive 1 — no double-sell (concurrency control).** Two buyers grabbing the same seat is a write conflict. Use the taught **concurrency-control** options: pessimistic `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` on the seat row (contention is high during a flash sale), or optimistic version-check-and-retry. The winning phrasing: give each seat a single owner via the row lock rather than a fragile distributed lock.

**Deep dive 2 — seat-hold TTL (the key deep dive).** A hold reserves a seat temporarily so a user can pay, but an abandoned hold must not lock the seat forever — so a hold carries a **TTL** (same reasoning as a Redis lock with a TTL so a crashed holder doesn't block others). On expiry the seat returns to available. Flash-sale traffic hits the **cache/read-replica** browse path, protecting the CP booking core.

Taught in: CAP and PACELC; SQL vs NoSQL; Concurrency control (optimistic, pessimistic & distributed locks); Connection pooling & read replicas; Caching.

drills.title: Design a Metrics Monitoring / Observability System
drills.prompt: Design a system ingesting high-frequency time-series metrics from many hosts, supporting range-aggregation queries and threshold-based alerting, with bounded long-term storage growth.
drills.notes: Write-heavy, read-light -- opposite skew from most consumer systems in this list. Downsampling/rollup policy is the core scaling lever.
drills.solution:
**Requirements.** Functional: ingest high-frequency time-series metrics from many hosts, run range-aggregation queries, fire threshold alerts. Non-functional: **write-heavy, read-light** (the opposite skew from most consumer systems), bounded long-term storage growth.

**Core entities + API.** `Metric{name, tags, ts, value}`.
```
POST /ingest [samples]     (very high volume)
GET  /query?metric&range&agg
```

**High-level design.** Ingest through a **stream (Kafka)** to absorb the write firehose with **backpressure**, then **workers** write to a time-series store. Because the workload is write-dominated, the taught **SQL-vs-NoSQL** reasoning points at a **wide-column** store (huge write throughput, query-first schema) partitioned by `(metric, time-bucket)`.

**Deep dive 1 — partition key & hot partitions.** Per the taught partitioning lesson, partition by metric plus a **time bucket** so writes spread and the *current* bucket doesn't become an unbounded **hot partition**. Recent data is the hot read path; put a small **cache** in front of dashboard queries.

**Deep dive 2 — bounded storage via downsampling (the core scaling lever).** Raw high-resolution samples can't be kept forever. Roll up old data to coarser resolution (per-minute → per-hour → per-day) and expire raw samples with a retention **TTL** — the same time-vs-cost tradeoff as cache invalidation, applied to storage. **Estimation** earns its keep here: samples/sec × bytes × retention tells you directly whether raw data fits on one node or must be partitioned and downsampled. Alerting is a stream consumer evaluating thresholds; delivery is at-least-once, so alert handlers must be **idempotent**.

Taught in: Message queues and streams; Replication and partitioning; SQL vs NoSQL; Caching; Estimation, only when it changes the design.

drills.title: Design a Distributed Cache
drills.prompt: Design the caching infrastructure itself (think: build a simplified Redis/Memcached) -- GET/SET/DELETE with TTL, horizontally scalable, tolerant of node failure.
drills.notes: Consistent hashing with virtual nodes is the centerpiece. Different problem shape than 'add a cache to your design' -- here the cache IS the design.
drills.solution:
**Requirements.** Functional: `GET/SET/DELETE` with TTL, as a service. Non-functional: horizontally scalable across nodes, tolerant of node failure, fast. (The cache *is* the design here, not an add-on.)

**Core entities + API.**
```
GET key -> value | miss
SET key value [ttl]
DELETE key
```

**High-level design.** Data is spread across many cache nodes. A client (or a proxy) hashes the key to pick the owning node. Naive `hash(key) % N` is fatal: change `N` (add/remove a node) and nearly every key remaps at once — a cache stampede against the backing DB.

**Deep dive 1 — consistent hashing (the centerpiece).** Place nodes and keys on a hash ring; a key is owned by the next node clockwise. Adding or removing a node **remaps only the adjacent range**, not the whole keyspace — exactly the taught load-balancing "consistent hashing sticks a key to the same server" point, here as the sharding scheme. Add **virtual nodes** (many ring points per physical node) so load is even and a removed node's keys spread across many survivors instead of dumping on one neighbour.

**Deep dive 2 — TTL, eviction & fault tolerance.** Entries carry a **TTL** and expire lazily/actively; when memory is full, evict by policy (LRU). This is the taught caching lesson's own machinery (TTL-based invalidation, thundering-herd risk when a hot key expires — mitigate with a short repopulation lock or randomized TTLs). Fault tolerance: replicate each key to the next node(s) on the ring so a node failure doesn't lose its whole range — the taught **replication** idea (copies of the same data) layered on top of partitioning.

Taught in: Load balancers & reverse proxies (consistent hashing); Caching; Replication and partitioning.

drills.title: Design a ChatGPT-style RAG System
drills.prompt: Design a system that accepts a user prompt, optionally retrieves grounding context via vector similarity search, generates a response via an LLM, and streams tokens back in real time.
drills.notes: 2025-2026 addition to the standard curriculum. Know when retrieval is even needed, and pgvector-on-existing-DB vs dedicated vector DB as a first decision.
drills.solution:
**Requirements.** Functional: accept a prompt, optionally retrieve grounding context, generate a response via an LLM, stream tokens back in real time. Non-functional: low time-to-first-token, retrieve only when it helps, scale read-heavy similarity search.

**Core entities + API.** `Document/Chunk{id, text, embedding}`, `Query`.
```
POST /chat {prompt}  -> streamed tokens
```

**High-level design.** Two phases straight from the taught **vector-database** lesson:
- **Offline:** chunk the corpus, embed each chunk, index the vectors.
- **Online:** embed the query, retrieve **top-k similar** chunks via approximate nearest neighbour, feed prompt + retrieved docs to the LLM.
First decision: **is retrieval even needed?** If the prompt is self-contained, skip it — a taught point.

**Deep dive 1 — vector store choice (the first real decision).** The taught lesson's default is **pgvector on the Postgres you already have** ("don't add infra yet") for interview-scale corpora; reach for a dedicated vector DB (Pinecone/Weaviate) only when scale/QPS forces it. This is the SQL-vs-NoSQL discipline applied to embeddings: justify with the specific access pattern, not "it scales."

**Deep dive 2 — streaming delivery.** Tokens must appear as they're generated, so the response is a one-way server→client stream — **Server-Sent Events (SSE)**, which the real-time lesson names as the lighter choice when you don't need client→server on the same channel. Cache identical/embedding-equivalent queries (**cache-aside**) to cut cost and latency, and put a small queue in front of the LLM call for **backpressure** under load.


**Extra tradeoff.** Retrieval breadth vs prompt cost: a larger top-k grounds the answer better but inflates the LLM context (latency and token cost), so cap k and rely on good chunking rather than retrieving more.
Taught in: Vector databases; SQL vs NoSQL; Real-time delivery; Caching; Message queues and streams.

drills.title: Drill: CAP theorem feature-by-feature split
drills.prompt: For a system of your choice (e.g., Tinder or Ticketmaster), identify two features with opposite CAP tradeoffs and justify each choice in one sentence.
drills.notes: Practice saying 'consistency for X because Y, availability for Z because W' fluently -- this is a first-30-seconds-of-deep-dive skill.
drills.solution:
**Direct answer.** Pick one system and name two features with opposite CAP tradeoffs, each justified in one sentence, in the taught feature-terms style.

Example — **Ticketmaster**:
- *Seat booking is CP:* "Booking must be consistent, so during a partition I'd rather reject a write than risk double-selling a seat — a wrong answer is worse than no answer."
- *Event browsing is AP:* "Browsing must stay available, so I'll serve a slightly stale availability count rather than error out, and reconcile after."

Or **Tinder**:
- *Matching/messaging is CP-leaning:* a match must be agreed by both sides consistently.
- *Profile view counts / 'who liked you' badge is AP:* a stale count is harmless, downtime is not.

**Reasoning.** The taught CAP lesson says CAP only bites **during a partition**, when you must choose Consistency *or* Availability — you can't have both. The skill being drilled is saying it in **feature terms**, fluently, in the first 30 seconds of a deep dive: "consistency for X because a wrong answer is unacceptable; availability for Z because stale is fine but downtime isn't."

**The tradeoff (PACELC).** Even with **no** partition (the common case), you still trade **Latency vs Consistency**: a strongly consistent write needs a quorum round-trip, while a fast local write risks staleness. So the real everyday question isn't binary "CP or AP" — it's "how much staleness can this feature tolerate for how much latency?" Answer at the feature level, never for the whole system.


**Common miss.** Declaring the *whole system* CP or AP is the mid-level error; the skill is splitting it feature by feature and defending each in one sentence, because a real product almost always needs both postures at once.
Taught in: CAP and PACELC.

drills.title: Drill: choose a caching strategy and invalidation policy
drills.prompt: Given a read-heavy product catalog page, pick cache-aside vs write-through vs write-back and a concrete invalidation approach, and justify against the alternatives.
drills.notes: Common miss: saying 'add a cache' without naming the strategy or invalidation approach -- interviewers probe here.
drills.solution:
**Direct answer.** For a read-heavy product catalog page, use **cache-aside** with a **TTL plus explicit invalidation on write**.

**Reasoning.** Cache-aside is the taught default: the app checks the cache, and on a miss loads from the DB and populates the entry. It fits a read-heavy catalog because reads vastly outnumber writes, so most requests never touch the DB, and the cache only holds what's actually requested (no wasted warming).

Why not the alternatives (all taught):
- **Write-through** (write cache + DB together) keeps the cache consistent but slows every write and caches items that may never be read — wasteful for a catalog where writes are rare.
- **Write-back** (write cache, flush to DB later) is fast but risks **data loss on a crash** — unacceptable for catalog/price data you must not lose.

**Invalidation policy.** Product data changes occasionally, so a pure TTL alone serves stale prices until it expires. Use a **short-ish TTL as a safety net** *plus* **explicit invalidation** on the update path (bust the key when a product changes). The taught lesson's exact point: most systems combine TTL with explicit invalidation on the paths that matter.

**The tradeoff.** Watch the **thundering herd**: when a hot key (a popular product) expires, thousands of requests miss at once and stampede the DB. Mitigate with a short lock on repopulation or slightly **randomized TTLs** so hot keys don't all expire together.


**Extra note.** Also decide *where* the cache sits: an application-tier Redis for the rendered catalog data, plus a CDN for the static images on the page — each layer catches what the layer above missed, and both use the same TTL-plus-invalidation reasoning.
Taught in: Caching.

drills.title: Drill: partition key design and hot partitions
drills.prompt: Design a partition key for a write-heavy, time-ordered dataset (e.g., chat messages or IoT sensor data) and explain how it could still produce a hot partition on reads, referencing the Discord case study.
drills.notes: A good write-distributing key can still be a bad read key. This is the exact lesson from Discord's (channel_id, bucket) design.
drills.solution:
**Direct answer.** For write-heavy, time-ordered data (chat messages, IoT sensor readings), partition by an entity id plus a **time bucket** — e.g. `(channel_id, day)` or `(sensor_id, hour)` — not by raw timestamp alone and not by id alone.

**Reasoning.** The taught replication-and-partitioning lesson: partitioning splits *different* data across nodes to scale writes, and the make-or-break choice is the **partition key**, which must spread load evenly *and* keep related data together. Partitioning by only a monotonic timestamp funnels every current write into one partition (a write hot spot). Partitioning by only `channel_id` lets one busy channel grow unbounded. Combining entity + time bucket spreads writes across entities and caps any single partition's size.

**The hot partition on reads (the sharp edge the prompt names).** A key that distributes **writes** well can still be a bad **read** key. Reads almost always want *recent* messages, so they concentrate on the **current** time bucket of the **most active** channel — a read **hot partition**, even though writes were balanced. This is exactly Discord's `(channel_id, bucket)` lesson: a huge popular channel hammers the newest bucket.

**Mitigations (all taught).** Add **read replicas** so the hot bucket's reads spread across copies; put a **cache** in front of the newest bucket (it's the hottest and most re-read); and size buckets so an active channel's current partition stays bounded.


**Extra note.** State the partition key by the access pattern it serves, never reflexively 'id'. If the dominant read is 'latest N for one entity', the time-bucket component is what keeps that read from scanning an ever-growing partition, and it also bounds each partition's size for compaction.
Taught in: Replication and partitioning; Connection pooling & read replicas; Caching.

drills.title: Drill: consistent hashing walkthrough
drills.prompt: Explain, step by step, what happens to key ownership when a node is added to a consistent-hashing ring with and without virtual nodes.
drills.notes: Be able to draw the ring and show only the adjacent range remaps -- not the whole keyspace.
drills.solution:
**Direct answer (step by step).** Consistent hashing places both nodes and keys on a hash ring (0…2^m). A key is owned by the **next node clockwise** from the key's hash.

**Without virtual nodes**, adding node **D** between C and A:
1. Compute `hash(D)`, place D on the ring.
2. Only the keys that fall in the arc **between D's predecessor and D** change ownership.
3. Those keys were previously served by the node clockwise of that arc (say A); now D serves them.
4. **Every other key stays put** — only the adjacent range remaps, not the whole keyspace.

Contrast with naive `hash(key) % N`: changing `N` remaps *nearly all* keys — the failure consistent hashing exists to prevent (a cache stampede against the DB).

**With virtual nodes**, each physical node is placed at **many** ring positions (e.g. 100 vnodes per node):
1. Adding D means inserting D's 100 vnodes scattered around the ring.
2. The keys D now owns are pulled from **many** predecessors, not one neighbour.
3. Result: load is **even** (no single neighbour dumps its whole range on the newcomer, and no unlucky node ends up with a giant arc), and when a node dies its keys **spread across many survivors** instead of doubling one neighbour's load.

**The tradeoff.** More vnodes → smoother balance and gentler failover, at the cost of more ring metadata to track. This is the taught mechanism behind "consistent hashing sticks a key to the same server," used for cache sharding and load distribution.

Taught in: Load balancers & reverse proxies (consistent hashing); Caching; Replication and partitioning.

drills.title: Drill: rate limiting algorithm comparison
drills.prompt: Compare token bucket, leaky bucket, and sliding window counter on burst tolerance, memory cost, and implementation complexity. Pick one for a public API and one for a payments webhook receiver.
drills.notes: Different systems legitimately want different algorithms -- avoid defaulting to 'token bucket' without reasoning.
drills.solution:
**Direct answer.** Compare the three taught algorithms, then pick per system.

| Algorithm | Burst tolerance | Memory cost | Complexity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Fixed window | Poor — allows ~2x at the boundary | Low (one counter/key) | Simplest |
| Sliding window | Good — smooths the boundary | Moderate | Medium |
| Token bucket | Tunable — bursts up to the cap | Low (tokens + timestamp) | Medium |

**Reasoning (from the taught rate-limiting lesson).**
- **Fixed window** counts per calendar interval; cheap, but a client can fire the full quota at the end of one window and again at the start of the next — a 2x boundary burst.
- **Sliding window** weights the previous window to smooth that boundary spike.
- **Token bucket** refills tokens at a steady rate up to a cap: **cap = burst tolerance, refill rate = sustained limit**. It permits short legitimate bursts while bounding sustained throughput.

**Picks.**
- *Public API:* **token bucket** — real clients are bursty (a page load fires several calls), and you want to allow short bursts while capping sustained abuse.
- *Payments webhook receiver:* **sliding window** (or a strict fixed cap) — you want a smooth, predictable ceiling and no boundary 2x spike hammering a sensitive downstream; bursts aren't a feature to reward here.

**Shared tradeoff.** Whatever you pick, the counters/buckets must live in **shared state (Redis)** — a per-server limit behind a load balancer isn't a real limit.

Taught in: Rate limiting; Load balancers & reverse proxies; Caching.

drills.title: Drill: SQL vs NoSQL justification with specifics
drills.prompt: For a given feature (e.g., user profiles vs. order transactions vs. activity feed), choose SQL or a specific NoSQL family (key-value/document/wide-column/graph) and justify with a concrete configuration detail, not just the family name.
drills.notes: Hello Interview explicitly flags 'I'll use NoSQL' with no specifics as a mid-level ceiling. Practice naming the specific tradeoff (e.g., partition key choice, consistency mode).
drills.solution:
**Direct answer.** Choose per feature with a concrete configuration detail, not just the family name:
- **User profiles →** document store (MongoDB): a profile is nested JSON fetched by user id as a unit; no joins.
- **Order transactions →** relational (Postgres): relationships (orders↔items↔payments) and **ACID transactions** — money and inventory can't be eventually consistent.
- **Activity feed →** wide-column (Cassandra/ScyllaDB): write-heavy, query-first, partitioned by `(user_id, time-bucket)`.

**Reasoning (from the taught SQL-vs-NoSQL lesson).** Choose on **data shape and access pattern**, not "NoSQL scales." Reach for relational when you have relationships, need joins, or need ACID (transactions), or when query patterns will evolve unpredictably — modern Postgres scales far further than folklore admits via read replicas and partitioning. Reach for NoSQL when the access pattern is known and simple (key/document by id), you need horizontal write scaling beyond one node, or the schema is genuinely flexible.

**Naming the specific tradeoff (what lifts this above a mid-level ceiling).** Hello Interview flags bare "I'll use NoSQL" as a mid-level ceiling. Strong answers name a config detail: "DynamoDB because the only access pattern is get-cart-by-user-id, writes are heavy, and I never join" — i.e. the **partition key** and the **consistency mode**. A useful tell from the lesson: if you find yourself wanting joins and transactions on a NoSQL store, you picked wrong.

**The tradeoff.** NoSQL buys write scale and flexible schema but costs you joins and (often) strong multi-row transactions; relational buys correctness and query flexibility but you scale it with replicas/partitioning rather than by adding nodes freely.

Taught in: SQL vs NoSQL; Replication and partitioning; Connection pooling & read replicas.

drills.title: Drill: back-of-envelope QPS and storage estimation
drills.prompt: Given 50M daily active users each performing 20 actions/day with a 3x peak multiplier, compute average QPS, peak QPS, and daily storage assuming 1KB per action record retained for 2 years with 3x replication.
drills.notes: Practice doing this in under 90 seconds. Remember Hello Interview's guidance: only bother with this in the real interview when a number would change your design.
drills.solution:
**Direct answer (do the math, ~90 seconds).**
- Actions/day = 50M users × 20 = **1e9 actions/day**.
- Average QPS = 1e9 / 86,400 s ≈ **~11,600 QPS**.
- Peak QPS = 3× average ≈ **~35,000 QPS**.
- Daily storage = 1e9 × 1 KB = **~1 TB/day**.
- 2-year raw = 1 TB/day × 730 ≈ **~730 TB**; × 3 replication ≈ **~2.2 PB**.

**Reasoning (from the taught estimation lesson).** Use the memorised anchors: ~1 req/user/day at 100M users ≈ ~1,150 QPS (so 50M × 20 scales to ~11.6K), peak is typically 2–3× average, and 1 KB × 1M writes/day ≈ 1 GB/day. The whole point is to reach a number that **changes a design decision** — here, ~2.2 PB over 2 years plainly does not fit one node, so it forces **partitioning** and a retention/downsampling policy; 35K peak QPS forces horizontal scaling and caching on the read path.

**The tradeoff (when to even do this).** The taught guidance: **skip the math unless a number will change your design**, and say so out loud. "How many bytes is a username?" doesn't move a box; "does the working set fit one in-memory node or must I shard?" does. Compute inline only when the result forces a decision (replication factor and retention are exactly such levers), and don't chase false precision — order-of-magnitude is the goal.


**Extra note.** Reads usually dominate writes 10:1 to 1000:1 for consumer products, so the ~35K peak is skewed toward reads — that decides you optimise the read path (caching, read replicas) first, and the ~2.2 PB decides you must partition. If the number didn't move either box, you'd skip the math entirely.
Taught in: Estimation, only when it changes the design; Replication and partitioning.

drills.title: Drill: Kafka partitioning and consumer group scaling
drills.prompt: Explain why adding a 5th consumer to a consumer group reading a 4-partition topic does not increase throughput, and what you'd change to fix that.
drills.notes: Partition count is the hard ceiling on intra-group consumer parallelism -- a very common gotcha question.
drills.solution:
**Direct answer.** Adding a 5th consumer to a group reading a **4-partition** topic gains nothing because **a partition is assigned to at most one consumer within a group**. With 4 partitions the group tops out at 4 active consumers; the 5th sits **idle** as a hot standby. To fix it, **increase the topic's partition count** (e.g. to 8) so consumer parallelism has room to grow.

**Reasoning (from the taught queues/streams lesson).** A Kafka topic is an append-only **log** split into partitions; consumers in a group divide the partitions among themselves so each message is processed once per group. **Partition count is the hard ceiling on intra-group consumer parallelism** — you scale consumers *up to* the partition count, not beyond. Ordering is preserved **per partition** (per-key ordering), which is why messages that must stay ordered share a key and thus a partition.

**The tradeoff.** More partitions raise the parallelism ceiling but aren't free: more partitions mean more open file handles/metadata, more rebalancing work, and — critically — **you can't cheaply reduce** partitions later, and re-partitioning changes which key lands where (breaking per-key ordering assumptions during the migration). So size partitions for your **peak** expected consumer parallelism up front. If reprocessing throughput (not ingestion) is the bottleneck, adding partitions plus consumers is the lever; if a single hot key dominates, more partitions won't help because that key's ordering pins it to one partition/consumer.


**Extra note.** Consumer parallelism is also bounded by keying: if throughput is fine but one key is slow, more partitions won't help because that key's ordering pins it to a single partition and consumer — the fix there is a different partition key, not more partitions.
Taught in: Message queues and streams.

drills.title: Drill: idempotency key design for a retryable write API
drills.prompt: Design the idempotency-key mechanism for a 'create order' API that may be retried by the client after a timeout. Specify what's stored, for how long, and what happens on a duplicate key with a different request body.
drills.notes: Directly modeled on Stripe's public design. Handling a duplicate key with a *different* payload (should this be an error?) is the sharp edge interviewers probe.
drills.solution:
**Direct answer.** For a retryable `create order` API, require a client-supplied **idempotency key** (e.g. a UUID the client generates once per logical order and reuses on retries). Store `key -> {status, response, request_fingerprint}`. On a **duplicate key with the same body**, return the **stored response** (don't create a second order). On a **duplicate key with a *different* body**, reject with a **422/409** — the key was reused for a different request, which is a client bug you must surface, not silently honour.

**What's stored and for how long.** Store the key, a hash/fingerprint of the request body, the resulting order id, and the final response. Keep it long enough to outlast realistic client retry windows — typically **~24 hours** via a **TTL** (same reasoning as any cache/lock TTL: bounded storage, and after that a retry is treated as a fresh request).

**Reasoning (from the taught lessons).** Networks give you **at-least-once** delivery: a client that times out doesn't know whether the write landed, so it retries — the exact at-least-once discipline the queues and webhooks lessons demand, where "your handler must be idempotent." The idempotency key turns an unsafe retry into a safe no-op. Concurrency matters too: two retries can race, so the **first insert of the key must be atomic** (unique constraint / `INSERT … ON CONFLICT`), which is the taught concurrency-control point — let the DB's uniqueness be the single owner rather than a distributed lock.

**The sharp edge.** The *different-payload-same-key* case is what interviewers probe: honouring it would corrupt data, so it must be an explicit error.

Taught in: Message queues and streams; TCP/UDP, HTTP/2 & 3, gRPC, webhooks; Concurrency control (optimistic, pessimistic & distributed locks).

drills.title: Drill: geospatial index selection
drills.prompt: Compare geohash, quadtree, and H3 for a 'find nearby restaurants' feature vs. a 'real-time driver dispatch' feature, and explain if the right choice differs between the two.
drills.notes: Uniform neighbor distance matters much more for dispatch/expansion algorithms than for a one-shot proximity search -- articulate why.
drills.solution:
**Direct answer.** For **"find nearby restaurants"** (a one-shot proximity search), geohash or a quadtree is fine — you look up the query cell and its neighbours and return matches. For **"real-time driver dispatch"**, prefer **H3 (hexagons)** because its **uniform neighbor distance** makes ring-by-ring outward expansion correct and cheap. So yes — the right choice **differs** between the two features.

**Reasoning.** All three bucket the map into cells and index entities by cell so a proximity query reads a handful of cells instead of scanning everyone — the taught idea of choosing an index/partition scheme by **access pattern**. The distinguishing factor:
- **Geohash** = string-prefix grid of lat/long rectangles; simple and range-scannable, but cells are **not** uniform in size or in neighbour distance (they distort toward the poles), and rectangular neighbours have unequal center distances.
- **Quadtree** = recursive square subdivision; adapts to density, but squares still have unequal diagonal-vs-edge neighbour distances.
- **H3** = hexagonal grid; every neighbour is (near) equidistant, which is what a dispatch algorithm needs when it expands the search radius ring by ring to find the closest available driver.

(Grounded via the drill's own Uber H3 source; the taught concept underneath is that dense cells become **hot partitions**, so whatever scheme you pick must spread load and you cache/replicate the hottest cells.)

**The tradeoff.** A one-shot "nearby" query doesn't care about neighbour uniformity, so pay nothing for H3's advantage — use the simplest indexable scheme. Dispatch's expansion search *does* care, so the uniform-distance property earns its complexity.

Taught in: Replication and partitioning; Caching; A framework that fits in 45 minutes.

drills.title: Drill: vector database vs. vector extension decision
drills.prompt: Given a 'similar products' recommendation feature with 2M product embeddings and moderate QPS, decide between pgvector-on-Postgres and a dedicated vector database like Pinecone, and state what scale/requirement would flip your answer.
drills.notes: The correct default answer for most interview-scale numbers is 'start with a vector extension on the DB I already have' -- know what would change that.
drills.solution:
**Direct answer.** For a "similar products" feature with **2M embeddings and moderate QPS**, start with **pgvector on the Postgres you already run**. Flip to a dedicated vector DB (Pinecone/Weaviate) when scale or requirements outgrow it — roughly: **hundreds of millions+ of vectors**, high QPS with strict low-latency SLAs, or heavy metadata-filtered ANN that your Postgres node can't serve alongside its normal load.

**Reasoning (from the taught vector-database lesson).** A vector DB stores embeddings and answers "find the k most similar vectors" via **approximate nearest neighbour (ANN)** indexes (e.g. HNSW). The lesson's explicit default for interview-scale numbers is **"don't add infra yet"**: 2M vectors at moderate QPS fits comfortably in pgvector, and you get to reuse your existing operational stack, backups, and — importantly — **join product metadata in the same query** instead of stitching two systems together. This is the **SQL-vs-NoSQL discipline** applied to embeddings: justify the choice with the specific access pattern and scale, not "a dedicated vector DB scales better."

**What flips the answer.** Corpus size beyond a single Postgres node's memory for the ANN index; QPS/latency SLAs that contend with your transactional workload on the same box (a dedicated store isolates that load); or advanced needs like sharded ANN, namespace isolation, or managed horizontal scaling. At that point the taught partitioning/replication reasoning says a purpose-built, independently scalable store earns its operational cost.

**The tradeoff.** pgvector = one less system, transactional consistency with your product data, joins for free — but bounded by one DB's resources. Dedicated vector DB = horizontal scale and isolation — at the cost of another system to run and keep in sync.

Taught in: Vector databases; SQL vs NoSQL; Replication and partitioning.

drills.title: Design an eval suite for a RAG chatbot
drills.prompt: You're given a customer-support RAG chatbot backed by a product knowledge base. Design an offline + online eval suite: what would you measure (retrieval quality vs. generation quality, separately), what your golden dataset looks like, how you'd catch regressions before deploy, and how you'd use LLM-as-judge safely given its known biases (position, recency, provenance).
drills.notes: Separate retrieval-quality metrics (recall@k, MRR) from generation metrics (faithfulness, relevance). Address LLM-judge bias mitigations explicitly: pairwise comparison, blinded provenance, judge-vs-human agreement check before trusting it at scale.
drills.solution:
**What it's testing:** Whether you separate the two halves of a RAG system when evaluating, and whether you treat an LLM judge as a measuring instrument that needs calibration rather than ground truth.

**Approach.** Evaluate retrieval and generation *separately* — conflating them hides which half is broken. For retrieval use recall@k and MRR (did the right chunks come back). For generation use faithfulness (is the answer grounded in the retrieved chunks) and relevance. Design across two axes: **offline** eval before deploy against a fixed set (golden examples, adversarial cases, regression cases harvested from past production failures), and **online** eval against live traffic (thumbs up/down, edits, re-asks, sampled human review). Neither substitutes for direct human inspection of real outputs.

**Catching regressions before deploy:** run the offline golden + regression set as a cheap pre-filter on every prompt/pipeline change, before spending live traffic.

**Using LLM-as-judge safely** given documented position, recency, and provenance biases: prefer *pairwise* comparison over pointwise scoring, *randomise order and blind provenance* before judging, *validate judge-vs-human agreement* on a labelled sample before trusting it at scale, and *re-run the judge on identical inputs* to measure its own variance before shipping it as a gate.

**Decision framework:** offline is necessary but not sufficient (sets go stale, can't anticipate every input); online is where the real rollout call is made. Use both plus manual inspection.

**Pitfalls:** a single blended "is the answer good" score that can't tell a retrieval miss from a bad generation; trusting judge scores without an agreement check; a golden set that doesn't cover real usage.

Taught in: Evals: the part everyone calls the hard part; LLM-as-judge and its pitfalls; RAG: grounding a model in your data.

drills.title: RAG vs. long context: make the call for a legal-document Q&A tool
